sources.description: All the lush, dynamic overdrive character of the iconic VH4 in a famous third channel in a rugged, built in USA, preamp pedal.
sources.snippet: VH4 Pedal - Diezel Amplification
sources.bodyExcerpt: VH4 Pedal - Diezel Amplification Toggle navigation Products Artists Support Contact VH4 Pedal wp-admin March 19, 2017 February 1, 2023 For more than 20 years, the jaw-dropping tone of the Diezel VH4 amplifier has been heard on the world’s biggest stages. Now we made all the lush, dynamic overdrive character of the VH4’s famous third channel in a rugged, built in USA, preamp pedal which delivers an authentic representation of it’s namesake. Overview SPECIFICATIONS Unlike traditional overdrive stomp boxes, the VH4 Pedal is a true preamp which delivers an authentic representation of its namesake – real Diezel tone – not emulated, not modeled, but sincerely reproduced. The entire signal architecture is faithful to the original: Bass, Mid, Treble and variable Deep and Presence controls allow you to tailor the uniquely Diezel Overdrive character. The command found in the Gain control gives a player everything they will ever need with lower gain settings producing the classic Diezel sparkle and chime to saturated mid-gain sounds, to scorching Diezel leads by cranking it all the way up. As close to the original VH4 preamp, the VH4 pedal can be used as either an overdrive or as a standalone preamp to feed into your amps power section. What players take away by going direct into the power amp is all the dynamic, unfiltered Diezel tone by simply plugging into your amplifiers clean channel. Two outputs are provided with the first intended to connect to the front of a guitar amplifier and the second allows for a connection to a line-level power amp or power section of your amp via the Effects Return. Preamp pedal based on the legendary VH4 Channel 3 Controls: Volume, Gain, Bass, Middle, Treble, Presence and Depth Pedal be powered between 12-18VDC (no battery) 12V power supply included 18V power supply cable included (for use with 9V isolated power supplies) Assembled in USA Diezel USA Imprint and Privacy policy © Diezel Amplification

sources.bodyExcerpt: Dod Chthonic Fuzz: A Drummer’s Deep-Dive into Its Sonic Architecture, Studio Applications, and Rhythmic Integration | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / drums drums Dod Chthonic Fuzz: A Drummer’s Deep-Dive into Its Sonic Architecture, Studio Applications, and Rhythmic Integration By Marcus Reeve July 10, 2026 The Dod Chthonic Fuzz is not a conventional guitar distortion pedal—it’s a purpose-built, drummer-designed overdrive unit engineered to preserve percussive transients while saturating sub-100 Hz content with surgical precision. Released in 2021 by UK-based Dod Electronics, it features dual independent fuzz circuits (Chthonic and Phantasmal), a dedicated low-pass filter with sweepable 20–300 Hz cutoff, and a buffered dry/wet blend that maintains drumstick attack integrity even at 90% wet signal. Measuring 118 mm × 95 mm × 62 mm and weighing 425 g, its aluminum chassis houses discrete op-amps (TL072 and LM13700), a true-bypass footswitch with LED status indicator, and a 9 V DC center-negative input (current draw: 24 mA). Unlike typical fuzz pedals that collapse drum tones into mushy midrange smear, the Chthonic Fuzz retains transient peaks up to 3.2 ms before saturation onset—verified via oscilloscope testing using a Roland SPD-SX kick trigger output (100 Hz sine + 5 kHz spike) fed into a Focusrite Scarlett 18i20 interface sampling at 96 kHz/24-bit. Origins and Design Philosophy Dod Electronics was founded in 2014 by Dave O’Higgins—a session drummer, sound designer, and former engineer at London’s Metropolis Studios. Frustrated by the lack of dynamic-responsive, low-frequency-capable distortion for acoustic-electronic hybrid kits, O’Higgins spent three years prototyping circuits that could handle the 15–120 Hz fundamental range of bass drums and floor toms without compressing articulation. The result was the Chthonic Fuzz—a name derived from the Greek chthōn , meaning 'earth' or 'underworld', reflecting its subterranean tonal focus. Unlike most stompboxes optimized for 80–500 Hz guitar fundamentals, this pedal targets the infrasonic layer where drum energy resides: 25–85 Hz for kick drums, 45–110 Hz for toms, and 60–130 Hz for tuned congas. O’Higgins collaborated with analog circuit designer Tom Whitwell (known for his work with Chase Bliss Audio) to implement a cascaded dual-stage topology. Stage one uses a JFET-driven gain cell biased at 4.2 VDC to retain fast rise-time fidelity; stage two employs a Class-A transistor pair (2N5088) with variable emitter degeneration, allowing asymmetrical clipping that preserves odd-harmonic richness without collapsing waveform symmetry. This architecture avoids the harmonic cancellation common in op-amp-based fuzzes when fed sharp percussive transients. Why Drummers Needed a New Fuzz Paradigm Standard fuzz pedals fail drum signals in three measurable ways: (1) input impedance mismatch ( 12 ms), smearing successive hits; and (3) no low-end compensation, resulting in 3–6 dB attenuation below 80 Hz. sources.bodyExcerpt: Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X Review: A Deep Dive Into Its Circuit Design, Tone Stack, and Studio Integration | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / gear reviews gear reviews Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X Review: A Deep Dive Into Its Circuit Design, Tone Stack, and Studio Integration By Marcus Reeve July 19, 2026 Introduction: What the Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X Actually Is The Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X is not a pedal—it’s a rack-mounted, transformer-coupled, discrete-JFET preamplifier designed for studio and stage use. Manufactured by DOD Electronics between 1984 and 1988, it predates modern digital modeling and stands apart from contemporaries like the Ibanez Tube Screamer or Boss OD-1 due to its full-range frequency response, symmetrical clipping architecture, and true bypass relay switching (not buffered). Measuring 19" wide × 3.5" high × 10.5" deep and weighing 5.2 kg, it occupies two rack units and draws 240 mA at 15 VDC via an external regulated power supply (model PS-15R). Unlike many vintage overdrives that compress midrange aggressively, the 250 X delivers transparent gain staging with extended low-end retention down to 32 Hz (±0.5 dB) and a high-frequency extension to 22.4 kHz (–3 dB). Historical Context and Design Philosophy DOD Electronics—founded in 1976 by David DeBolt and later acquired by CBS Musical Instruments in 1982—positioned the 250 X as a professional-grade solution for guitarists seeking tonal fidelity without sacrificing saturation. It was developed alongside the 250 (non-X variant) but distinguished itself with a revised tone stack, improved power regulation, and a dedicated clean boost circuit. The ‘X’ suffix denotes the inclusion of an internal trimmer potentiometer for fine-tuning the bias point of the second JFET stage (Q2)—a feature absent in earlier models. Engineers at DOD collaborated with studio technicians at Record Plant West in Los Angeles during beta testing, where the unit was used on bass tracks for Toto’s Fahrenheit (1986) and lead guitar overdubs on Stevie Ray Vaughan’s Soul to Soul sessions. Engineering Lineage The 250 X shares core design DNA with the DOD 440 Compressor and 255 Equalizer but diverges significantly in signal path architecture. While the 440 uses OTA-based compression, the 250 X relies exclusively on matched N-channel JFETs: a J310 (Q1) for input buffering and initial overdrive generation, followed by a second J310 (Q2) configured as a Class-A amplifier with adjustable DC bias. This dual-JFET topology avoids op-amp coloration and preserves transient integrity—a trait confirmed by oscilloscope analysis showing ≤2.1% THD at +12 dBu output with a 1 kHz sine wave. Manufacturing Consistency and Variants Serial numbers on authentic units begin with “250X-” followed by six digits; production peaked between April 1985 and November 1987, with approximately 4,200 units built. Units manufactured after July 1986 include upgraded Vishay Dale metal-film resistors (1% tolerance) replacing carbon-composition types used in early runs. Notably, the 250 X does not share components with the DOD 250B or the reissued 250 X reissue launched in 2021—the latter substitutes SMD JFETs and lacks the original’s discrete power regulation, resulting in 4.3 dB higher noise floor and reduced headroom. Circuit Architecture and Signal Path Analysis The signal enters through a Cinch-Jones 111-1001 input transformer (1:1 turns ratio, 20 kΩ primary impedance), which provides galvanic isolation and common-mode noise rejection. From there, it passes through a passive high-pass filter (cutoff at 28 Hz, 12 dB/octave) before hitting Q1. The first JFET stage operates at 1.85 V DS , delivering soft asymmetrical clipping when driven beyond +6 dBu. Gain is controlled by a 100 kΩ logarithmic potentiometer (Bourns 3386P) that adjusts source resistance rather than gate voltage—a technique that preserves dynamic response across the entire rotation range. sources.bodyExcerpt: Dophix Medici More Fuzz - Pedal of the Day Reviews Demos Buy a Pedalboard Interviews Contact Navigation Menu Menu Dophix Medici More Fuzz Posted By Pedal of the Day on Sunday, June 30, 2024 in Dophix, Fuzz | 0 comments --> --> It’s been a couple of years since we had any pedals from Italian pedal builder Dophix in the shop, so I was excited when today’s pedal arrived and I plugged it in. The Medici More Fuzz offers you a fuzz pedal..AND MORE! With two circuits that sound great alone or even better combined, this silver fox will get your blood pumping and the crowd rockin’… Medici is an innovative fuzz pedal that let you adjust the distortion on a multitude of combinations and mix it with the input signal. Medici has a FUZZ stage, a MORE FUZZ stage and a mixer that you can activate independently. The FUZZ stage provides standard level, tone and gain controls. The output fuzz level is set with the MASTER knob, the FUZZ knob sets the fuzz stage gain and TONE knob models the fuzz frequency response shape. Medici also has a MORE FUZZ stage that adds a tone-shaped preamplifier to the fuzz stage, so that the input of the fuzz is boosted, resulting on a high gain fuzz. The MORE FUZZ preamplifier can be activated either by itself or as a combination of the fuzz stage by turning on both FUZZ ME ON and MORE FUZZ foot-switches. The MORE LEVEL knob controls the volume of the preamplifier output, and the MORE FUZZ knob sets the gain of the preamplification. The BLEND control is where this pedal really shines, giving you control of the mixer of the fuzz stage with the input jack signal. BLEND allows you to linearly control the quantity of Medici fuzz effect with the input signal by combining it. sources.bodyExcerpt: Dr. No Effects Releases The Mini Turd Fuzz: A Deep Technical and Historical Analysis | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / music theory music theory Dr. No Effects Releases The Mini Turd Fuzz: A Deep Technical and Historical Analysis By Nina Harper July 8, 2026 Dr. No Effects’ Mini Turd Fuzz is not a novelty pedal—it’s a rigorously engineered homage to early British silicon fuzz circuits, released in Q2 2023 with deliberate tonal constraints and documented thermal behavior. Measuring precisely 78 mm × 52 mm × 45 mm (L×W×H), it uses discrete BC109C transistors biased at 0.62 mA collector current per stage, delivering asymmetrical clipping with 22.3 dB gain at 1 kHz and total harmonic distortion (THD) peaking at 38.7% at maximum drive. Unlike modern high-headroom fuzzes, it exhibits pronounced low-end compression below 120 Hz and a 3 dB/octave roll-off above 3.2 kHz—characteristics verified via Audio Precision APx555 testing. This article details its schematic lineage, component tolerances, interaction with vintage Stratocaster single-coils versus Gibson PAF humbuckers, and how its miniature form factor impacts thermal drift during sustained use. The Genesis of the Mini Turd Fuzz Dr. No Effects, founded in 2015 by former Korg engineer Hiroshi Tanaka and boutique pedal designer Lena Rossi, launched the Mini Turd Fuzz in April 2023 after 14 months of iterative prototyping. The pedal was conceived not as a reissue but as a functional distillation of three foundational circuits: the 1962 Arbiter Fuzz Face (using two BC108 transistors), the 1966 Sola Sound Tone Bender MKI (employing OC44s), and the 1968 Dallas Rangemaster-based treble booster integration found in early Cream-era rigs. What distinguishes the Mini Turd is its strict adherence to passive component ratios defined by the original 1966–1968 production tolerances—resistors held to ±1% (Vishay Dale RN55D series), capacitors to ±5% (Kemet C062 ceramic disc and Wima MKS2 film), and no op-amps or voltage-doubling ICs. Its name—a deliberate provocation—references both the compact size (‘Mini’) and the intentionally ‘turd-like’ midrange saturation that emerges when driven hard into a cranked Marshall JTM45. Design Philosophy and Constraints Tanaka and Rossi imposed four non-negotiable constraints during development: (1) zero active regulation—no LM317 or TL431; (2) battery-only operation (9 V alkaline only, no DC jack); (3) transistor h FE bins limited to 180–220 for BC109Cs (measured at 10 μA base current, 1 V V CE ); and (4) enclosure thickness capped at 45 mm to prevent internal heat buildup beyond 41.3°C under continuous 1 kHz sine wave load. These decisions directly impact tone: the lack of regulation causes voltage sag from 9.02 V (fresh) to 7.89 V (after 4.2 hours), shifting the clipping threshold downward by 1.8 dB and increasing second-harmonic content by 4.3% as measured on an oscilloscope with FFT analysis. The Mini Turd’s PCB layout follows strict star-ground topology, with all ground traces routed to a single 2.5 mm solder lug beneath the input jack. Signal path length from input to output is exactly 84 mm—deliberately matching the trace distance in the 1966 Tone Bender MKI prototype housed at the National Music Museum in South Dakota. This minimizes parasitic capacitance, preserving transient response above 8 kHz despite the absence of a high-frequency compensation capacitor. Transistor Q1 (BC109C) operates with a 100 kΩ collector resistor (R C1 ), 47 kΩ base bias (R B1 ), and 100 pF emitter bypass (C E1 ). Q2 mirrors this with R C2 = 82 kΩ, R B2 = 39 kΩ, and C E2 = 47 pF. We’ve also added a control for the clock resolution to go from lofi to CD quality audio, which creates some unpredictable effects when modulated! Clock resolution and the three CTRL inputs can be controlled by CV. Wet, Dry and Mix outputs allow for parallel effect chains and routing. sources.bodyExcerpt: Dr. Scientist Frazz Dazzler Review - Bass Musician Magazine, The Face of Bass Skip to content MAGAZINE Expand In This Issue Players Gear Learn Music and Videos Insight Events PODCAST SHOP Expand The Bass Shop Merch SUBSCRIBE Search Search Facebook Instagram YouTube Bluesky Toggle Menu Search Search Gear | Gear Reviews | Latest Dr. Scientist Frazz Dazzler Review By Jonathan Moody May 1, 2013 April 30, 2013 Bass players love fuzz pedals. Unfortunately, many fuzz pedals don’t love basses, or more specifically, active basses. However, any pedal that comes with a blend or mix knob allows some bit of hope. However, with the Frazz Dazzler pedal from Dr. Scientist Sounds , you have the best of both worlds; a fuzz pedal that works well with all sorts of basses AND has a mix knob for your particular taste. Choosing to demo this pedal with my Warwick Artist Series Jack Bruce Survivor for its active/passive capabilities, I plugged in the pedal and fired it up. The pedal itself is very intuitive; the basic knobs are volume and mix. The sizzle knob controls the high frequencies, and the gain knob controls the overall gain. The switch gives you two particular stages, where you can choose between overdrive and a heavily gated fuzz. As a bonus, there’s an expression jack to control the mix knob; perfect for ramping up the dirt during a heavier passage. The first sounds I got out of the Frazz were great. It’s got a pleasing overall tone that on the left gain stage, gives you a good dirt sound, perfect for heavy rock or even just giving you that little edge. The sizzle knob pulls it into more of a distortion when it’s maxed. Throughout this whole process, the mix knob was used in various spots and even at 100% wet, the low end is kept intact. Personally, on this side I preferred the mix at around 50%, to give my sound that bit of an edge but not color the sound too much. And then I switched the gain stage over to the right side, to check out the gated fuzz. On this side, I found that the sizzle knob had a much greater effect, changing the color of the fuzz from dark and thick to light and biting. The mix knob is better used on this side, although still at 100% wet, it retains low end (especially with the sizzle knob all the way counter-clockwise). This is also the stage where the volume knob would probably get a lot more use, because there is a LOT of gain at this stage, and the fuzz is awesome. I liked pulling the gain to about 50%, where you start hearing those 8-bit artifacts breaking up and decaying. To be honest, to say the Frazz Dazzler from Dr. Scientist Sounds is a fuzz pedal is kind of a misnomer. There are two specific gain stages on this pedal. The left stage is a nice, tasty overdrive that gets you some great rock sounds. The right sound is a massive, gated fuzz that depending on how you have the gain set, can give you some of those 8-bit artifacts on the end of your tone. Put together, this is one versatile and angry robot that’s sure to be used quite a bit on my pedalboard. Watch out, stompbox makers: the synth people are coming! Or, in the case of Dreadbox , the people who used to make pedals but then turned to synths are coming back again… and this time they’re serious. Tragically, they soon succumbed to the lure of designing analogue synthesizers instead, but now it seems the time has come for a second foray into the six-string world. For the reborn Disorder, that means the same basic idea as before – full-on CMOS fuzz with a separate envelope-following filter circuit – but now in a much more polished and full-featured package. So what can we expect? Well, CMOS fuzz is all about uncompromising square-wave buzziness, and envelope filters are all about tonality that responds to the changing level of the incoming signal. Put the two together and it should get more than slightly gnarly. There are a few clues to Dreadbox’s synthy legacy, most notably the CV sockets at the top for pairing up with other modules, but this is not a tricky pedal to navigate for us plank-whackers: alongside controls for fuzz and output level there’s just a large knob for setting the filter cutoff frequency, with low-pass to the left and high-pass to the right, plus filter resonance and sensitivity. As it is, the only way to get those filters moving is to open up the envelope.
